fetched_contents.text: Vitamin C and Immune Function Abstract Vitamin C is an essential micronutrient for humans, with pleiotropic functions related to its ability to donate electrons. It is a potent antioxidant and a cofactor for a family of biosynthetic and gene regulatory enzymes. Vitamin C contributes to immune defense by supporting various cellular functions of both the innate and adaptive immune system. Vitamin C supports epithelial barrier function against pathogens and promotes the oxidant scavenging activity of the skin, thereby potentially protecting against environmental oxidative stress. Vitamin C accumulates in phagocytic cells, such as neutrophils, and can enhance chemotaxis, phagocytosis, generation of reactive oxygen species, and ultimately microbial killing. It is also needed for apoptosis and clearance of the spent neutrophils from sites of infection by macrophages, thereby decreasing necrosis/NETosis and potential tissue damage. The role of vitamin C in lymphocytes is less clear, but it has been shown to enhance differentiation and proliferation of B- and T-cells, likely due to its gene regulating effects. Vitamin C deficiency results in impaired immunity and higher susceptibility to infections. In turn, infections significantly impact on vitamin C levels due to enhanced inflammation and metabolic requirements. Furthermore, supplementation with vitamin C appears to be able to both prevent and treat respiratory and systemic infections. Prophylactic prevention of infection requires dietary vitamin C intakes that provide at least adequate, if not saturating plasma levels (i.e., 100–200 mg/day), which optimize cell and tissue levels. In contrast, treatment of established infections requires significantly higher (gram) doses of the vitamin to compensate for the increased inflammatory response and metabolic demand. Keywords: ascorbate, ascorbic acid, immunity, immune system, neutrophil function, microbial killing, lymphocytes, infection, vitamin C 1. Introduction The immune system is a multifaceted and sophisticated network of specialized organs, tissues, cells, proteins, and chemicals, which has evolved in order to protect the host from a range of pathogens, such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, as well as cancer cells [1]. It can be divided into epithelial barriers, and cellular and humoral constituents of either innate (non-specific) and acquired (specific) immunity [1]. These constituents interact in multiple and highly complex ways. More than half a century of research has shown vitamin C to be a crucial player in various aspects of the immune system, particularly immune cell function [2,3]. Vitamin C is an essential nutrient which cannot be synthesized by humans due to loss of a key enzyme in the biosynthetic pathway [4,5]. Severe vitamin C deficiency results in the potentially fatal disease scurvy [6]. Scurvy is characterized by weakening of collagenous structures, resulting in poor wound healing, and impaired immunity. Individuals with scurvy are highly susceptible to potentially fatal infections such as pneumonia [7]. In turn, infections can significantly impact on vitamin C levels due to enhanced inflammation and metabolic requirements. Early on, it was noted that scurvy often followed infectious epidemics in populations [7], and cases of scurvy have been reported following respiratory infection [8]. This is particularly apparent for individuals who are already malnourished. Although the amount of vitamin C required to prevent scurvy is relatively low (i.e., ~10 mg/day) [9], the recommended dietary intakes for vitamin C are up to one hundred-fold higher than that for many other vitamins [10]. A diet that supplies 100–200 mg/day of vitamin C provides adequate to saturating plasma concentrations in healthy individuals and should cover general requirements for the reduction of chronic disease risk [11,12]. Due to the low storage capacity of the body for the water-soluble vitamin, a regular and adequate intake is required to prevent hypovitaminosis C. Epidemiological studies have indicated that hypovitaminosis C (plasma vitamin C < 23 μmol/L) is relatively common in Western populations, and vitamin C deficiency (<11 μmol/L) is the fourth leading nutrient deficiency in the United States [13,14]. There are several reasons why vitamin C dietary recommendations are not met, even in countries where food availability and supply would be expected to be sufficient. These include poor dietary habits, life-stages and/or lifestyles either limiting intakes or increasing micronutrient requirements (e.g., smoking and alcohol or drug abuse), various diseases, exposure to pollutants and smoke (both active and passive), and economic reasons (poor socioeconomic status and limited access to nutritious food) [15,16]. Even otherwise ‘healthy’ individuals in industrialized countries can be at risk due to lifestyle-related factors, such as those on a diet or eating an unbalanced diet, and people facing periods of excessive physical or psychological stress [15,16]. Vitamin C has a number of activities that could conceivably contribute to its immune-modulating effects. It is a highly effective antioxidant, due to its ability to readily donate electrons, thus protecting important biomolecules (proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, and nucleic acids) from damage by oxidants generated during normal cell metabolism and through exposure to toxins and pollutants (e.g., cigarette smoke) [17]. Vitamin C is also a cofactor for a family of biosynthetic and gene regulatory monooxygenase and dioxygenase enzymes [18,19]. The vitamin has long been known as a cofactor for the lysyl and prolyl hydroxylases required for stabilization of the tertiary structure of collagen, and is a cofactor for the two hydroxylases involved in carnitine biosynthesis, a molecule required for transport of fatty acids into mitochondria for generation of metabolic energy (Figure 1) [19]. fetched_contents.text: Complementary and Integrative Health Approaches to Travel Wellness | Yellow Book Introduction Travelers often ask their healthcare professional about the use of complementary or integrative health approaches for travel-related illnesses and conditions. Claims made about dietary supplements, herbal products (Box 1.13.1), and other complementary approaches for travel-related health problems may not be supported by evidence. Be prepared to discuss what is known about the benefits of complementary and integrative health approaches and to counsel travelers on their possible side effects or interactions with medications. Box 1.13.1 Dietary supplements and unproven therapies Unproven therapies are discussed in this section only for educational purposes and are not recommended for use. CDC only endorses therapies approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). FDA regulates dietary supplements, but the regulations are generally less strict than those for prescription or over-the-counter drugs. Clinicians and travelers should consult the FDA's safety advisories to learn the latest regarding product recalls and safety alerts. Two major safety concerns about dietary supplements are potential drug interactions and product contamination. Analyses of supplements sometimes find differences between labeled and actual ingredients. For example, products marketed as dietary supplements have been found to contain illegal hidden ingredients such as prescription drugs. Claims vs science Altitude illness prevention and treatment Many natural products, including coca leaf, garlic, Ginkgo biloba, and vitamin E, have been promoted for preventing or treating altitude illness. Coca leaf Coca leaf, chewed or made into tea, has been used for altitude illness, but no strong evidence has shown that it works or that it has adverse effects. Travelers should be aware that using coca leaf may cause a positive drug test result for cocaine metabolites. Garlic No evidence supports claims that garlic helps reduce altitude illness. Garlic supplements appear safe for most adults. Possible side effects include breath and body odor, heartburn, and upset stomach. Some people have allergic reactions to garlic. Short-term use of most commercially available garlic supplements poses only a limited risk for drug interactions. Ginkgo biloba Studies of Ginkgo biloba for preventing altitude illness are inadequate to justify recommendations about its use. Products made from standardized ginkgo leaf extracts appear to be safe when used as directed. However, ginkgo can increase the risk of bleeding in some people and can interact with anticoagulants. In addition, studies by the National Toxicology Program showed that rodents developed liver and thyroid tumors after being given a ginkgo extract for up to 2 years. Vitamin E One study investigated vitamin E in combination with other antioxidants for altitude illness; no significant benefit was observed. Colds and influenza Although colds and influenza are not uniquely travel-related hazards, many people try to avoid these illnesses during a trip. Complementary health approaches that have been advocated for preventing or treating colds or influenza include echinacea, elderberry, garlic and other herbs, nasal saline irrigation, probiotics, silver, South African geranium, vitamin C, and zinc products. Echinacea A 2023 systematic review and analysis concluded that echinacea may improve cold symptoms; however, the quality of the evidence was low to moderate. Taking echinacea for a short amount of time is probably safe, but some people may experience gastrointestinal side effects. Elderberry Taking elderberry may be helpful for cold and influenza symptoms and may result in a quicker recovery from illness. However, the quality of the evidence is low because only a few small studies have been conducted. Elderberry flowers and ripe fruit appear to be safe, but the bark, leaves, seeds, and raw or unripe fruit can be toxic and cause gastrointestinal distress. Garlic and other herbs No strong evidence supports claims that on their own, garlic, Chinese herbs, oil of oregano, and eucalyptus essential oil prevent or treat colds, or that the homeopathic product Oscillococcinum prevents or treats influenza or influenza-like illness. A 2022 review of homeopathic products for colds in children did not find consistent evidence of benefit. Nasal saline irrigation Nasal saline irrigation (e.g., use of neti pots) can be useful and safe for chronic sinusitis. Nasal saline irrigation also can help relieve the symptoms of acute upper respiratory tract infections, but the evidence is not definitive. Even in places where tap water is safe to drink, people should use only sterile, distilled, boiled-then-cooled, or specially filtered water for nasal irrigation to avoid the risk of introducing waterborne pathogens. Probiotics Probiotics might reduce susceptibility to colds, influenza, or other upper respiratory tract infections and shorten the duration and severity of the illnesses. Effects were relatively consistent across different combinations of probiotics, doses, and durations, but the quality of the evidence is low. fetched_contents.text: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold Abstract Background Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) for preventing and treating the common cold has been a subject of controversy for 70 years. Objectives To find out whether vitamin C reduces the incidence, the duration or severity of the common cold when used either as a continuous regular supplementation every day or as a therapy at the onset of cold symptoms. Search methods We searched CENTRAL 2012, Issue 11, MEDLINE (1966 to November week 3, 2012), EMBASE (1990 to November 2012), CINAHL (January 2010 to November 2012), LILACS (January 2010 to November 2012) and Web of Science (January 2010 to November 2012). We also searched the U.S. National Institutes of Health trials register and WHO ICTRP on 29 November 2012. Selection criteria We excluded trials which used less than 0.2 g per day of vitamin C and trials without a placebo comparison. We restricted our review to placebo‐controlled trials. Data collection and analysis Two review authors independently extracted data. We assessed 'incidence' of colds during regular supplementation as the proportion of participants experiencing one or more colds during the study period. 'Duration' was the mean number of days of illness of cold episodes. Main results Twenty‐nine trial comparisons involving 11,306 participants contributed to the meta‐analysis on the risk ratio (RR) of developing a cold whilst taking vitamin C regularly over the study period. In the general community trials involving 10,708 participants, the pooled RR was 0.97 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.94 to 1.00). Five trials involving a total of 598 marathon runners, skiers and soldiers on subarctic exercises yielded a pooled RR of 0.48 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.64). A mini-report on daily vitamin C dosage, safety, and practical advice

## Recommended daily intakes for adults and vulnerable groups

The evidence points to a range of recommended intakes depending on age, sex, and life stage. The NIH ODS fact sheet states that adult requirements range from 90 to 120 mg for adults and from 15 to 115 mg for infants, children, and adolescents, with the exact amount depending on age, sex, and life stage [N2-R1]. The NHS also states that adults aged 19 to 64 need 40 mg/day, and that this amount should typically be obtainable from diet [N2-R3]. In contrast, the Linus Pauling Institute recommends 400 mg/day for adults to ensure replete tissue concentrations [N2-R2]. These differences reflect varying assumptions about how much vitamin C is needed for general health versus higher tissue concentrations.

For vulnerable groups, the evidence is less explicit in the provided search results, but the general message is that dietary intake is usually sufficient for most adults, with higher doses occasionally used to achieve repletion [N2-R3][N2-R2]. The CDC’s travel wellness section notes that vitamin C supplements are promoted for colds and influenza, but it explicitly warns that such claims may not be supported by evidence and that travelers should consult FDA safety advisories [N3-F2]. That context is useful for practical advice, especially for people using supplements in high-risk settings.

## Signs of deficiency and how much supplementation is typically used

Vitamin C deficiency is linked to impaired immunity and increased susceptibility to infections [N1-F1]. In the review, scurvy is described as a potentially fatal disease caused by severe deficiency, with symptoms including weakened collagen structures, poor wound healing, and impaired immunity [N1-F1]. The same review also notes that hypovitaminosis C (plasma vitamin C < 23 μmol/L) is relatively common in Western populations, and deficiency (<11 μmol/L) is the fourth leading nutrient deficiency in the United States [N1-F1]. These findings support the idea that deficiency is not rare and can have significant health consequences.

In practice, supplementation doses vary widely. The NIH and NHS evidence suggest routine intakes around 40–120 mg/day for most adults, while the Linus Pauling Institute recommends 400 mg/day for repletion [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R2]. The CDC’s travel wellness section also says that people may use vitamin C regularly, but it emphasizes that such use is not evidence-based and should be discussed with a provider [N3-F2]. So, typical supplementation is often higher than routine dietary needs, especially when people are trying to boost immunity or cover gaps in diet.

## Safety concerns for high doses and special populations

The evidence on safety is cautiously positive but not universal. WebMD states that the safe upper limit is 2,000 mg/day and that 500 mg/day is considered safe with a strong evidence track record [N2-R4]. The NIH ODS fact sheet also notes that the upper limit is 2,000 mg/day [N2-R1]. These are the strongest safety statements in the provided material.

Still, high doses can matter. The CDC’s travel wellness section warns about potential drug interactions and product contamination, including the possibility that supplements may contain illegal hidden ingredients such as prescription drugs [N3-F2]. It also highlights that analyses sometimes find differences between labeled and actual ingredients, and that some products may have side effects such as gastrointestinal upset, allergic reactions, or interactions with medications [N3-F2]. These concerns are especially relevant for special populations, including people on medications, those with chronic conditions, and pregnant or breastfeeding individuals, even though the provided evidence does not give explicit numbers for those groups.

In short, vitamin C is generally safe at moderate doses, but high-dose supplementation should be approached with care, and vulnerable individuals should consult a healthcare provider before using large amounts [N2-R4][N3-F2]. The practical advice is: aim for diet-first, use supplements only when needed, and keep doses below 2,000 mg/day unless a provider says otherwise [N2-R1][N2-R4].

A mini-report on what vitamin C does not do and common misconceptions

## Why vitamin C is not a proven cure or standalone treatment for infections

The evidence is clear that vitamin C is not a cure or standalone treatment for infections. The Cochrane review states that regular supplementation reduces cold duration but does not reduce incidence in the general population [N6-R4]. The CDC’s travel wellness section similarly says that vitamin C supplements are promoted for colds and influenza, but that claims may not be supported by evidence and are not recommended as proven interventions [N3-F2]. In other words, vitamin C can help in some ways, but it does not reliably prevent infections in the average person [N6-R4][N3-F2].

The same review also shows that therapeutic use after symptom onset has not consistently reduced cold duration or severity [N3-F3]. That means people should not assume that taking vitamin C at the first sign of illness will cure an infection on its own. The strongest evidence is for reduced duration and severity in regular supplementation studies, not for a cure or replacement for standard care [N3-F3][N6-R4].

## How diet, stress, and other factors affect immune response

The evidence repeatedly points to diet as a major determinant of immune status. The vitamin C and immune function review states that dietary intake of 100–200 mg/day provides adequate to saturating plasma concentrations and should cover general requirements [N1-F1]. It also notes that infections can significantly impact vitamin C levels due to enhanced inflammation and metabolic requirements, and that hypovitaminosis C is relatively common in Western populations [N1-F1]. This means that a poor diet can make immune defenses weaker even when vitamin C is not deliberately lacking.

Stress is also a relevant factor. The review says that otherwise healthy individuals in industrialized countries can be at risk due to lifestyle-related factors, including periods of excessive physical or psychological stress [N1-F1]. The CDC’s travel wellness section similarly frames travelers’ health in the context of stress and travel-related risks [N3-F2]. So, immune response is not only about vitamin C alone; it is shaped by overall diet quality, stress, and other environmental and lifestyle factors [N1-F1][N3-F2].

## Common misunderstandings about immune-boosting supplements

The evidence highlights several common misunderstandings. First, many people believe that vitamin C can prevent any illness, but the Harvard Health article explicitly states there is no evidence that large doses prevent one—or any other type of illness [N4-R3]. Second, the CDC’s travel wellness section warns that unproven therapies are discussed for educational purposes only and are not recommended [N3-F2]. This is important because it counters the idea that all complementary or integrative health approaches are safe or effective.

Third, the evidence shows that some claims about immune-boosting supplements are overstated. The Yellow Book notes that garlic, echinacea, elderberry, and other herbs are promoted for colds and influenza, but the evidence for most of them is weak or inconsistent [N3-F2]. Similarly, the review of vitamin C for colds says that only a few therapeutic trials have been carried out and that further RCTs are needed to settle the possible role of therapeutic vitamin C [N3-F3]. So, the common misconception is that supplements can reliably “boost” immunity in a direct, measurable way when the evidence is actually mixed or insufficient [N3-F2][N3-F3][N4-R3].

Overall, vitamin C is part of immune health, but it is not a magic bullet. Its real value lies in supporting normal immune function and reducing deficiency-related risk, not in curing or replacing standard medical care [N1-F1][N3-F2][N6-R4].

## Evidence for colds, respiratory infections, and other common infections

The evidence is strongest for colds and respiratory infections. The Cochrane review on vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold concludes that regular supplementation reduces cold duration, but does not reduce incidence in the general population [N6-R4]. The same review also notes that therapeutic trials have not consistently shown benefit [N3-F3]. A separate meta-analysis found that vitamin C significantly decreased the severity of the common cold by 15% [N6-R1], while another meta-analysis on vitamin C and the common cold found that it did not decrease the average number of colds in general community trials [N6-R2]. These findings show that the effect is mostly on duration and severity, not on preventing every cold.

For respiratory infections more broadly, the evidence is mixed but not entirely negative. The CDC’s travel wellness section notes that vitamin C supplements are promoted for colds and influenza, but it again warns that such claims may not be supported by evidence [N3-F2]. A separate search result also states that vitamin C and D supplementation reduce the risk of acute respiratory tract infections (ARIs), and that vitamin C and zinc supplementation shorten the duration of ARIs [N6-R3]. This is important because it expands the infection context beyond the common cold: respiratory infections more generally may show some benefit from combined micronutrient support, although the evidence for vitamin C alone is less strong [N6-R3].

There is also indirect evidence for other infections. The vitamin C and immune function review states that vitamin C deficiency results in impaired immunity and higher susceptibility to infections [N1-F1]. It also notes that infections can significantly impact vitamin C levels due to enhanced inflammation and metabolic requirements [N1-F1]. This means that vitamin C may matter for infections more broadly, especially when deficiency is present or when infection increases the body’s demand for the nutrient.

## Dose-response patterns and population-specific effects

The dose-response pattern is a key theme. In the Cochrane review, regular supplementation reduced cold duration by 8% in adults and 14% in children, with higher doses in children producing an additional 18% benefit [N3-F3]. The same review also found that in five trials involving participants exposed to extreme physical stress, vitamin C halved common cold risk [N3-F3]. So, the effect is not uniform: it appears stronger in children and in people under severe physical stress [N3-F3].

The dose-response relationship is also important for treatment. The review says that prophylactic prevention requires 100–200 mg/day to optimize cell and tissue levels, while treatment of established infections may require much higher doses [N1-F1]. This suggests that the same amount of vitamin C is not appropriate for prevention and treatment; the dose must match the purpose and the body’s needs [N1-F1].

Population-specific effects are also evident. The review notes that males require about 1.2-fold higher vitamin C intake than females to reach the same serum concentrations [N5-R3]. This implies that recommendations may need to be adjusted for sex, and that one-size-fits-all advice may not capture everyone’s needs [N5-R3]. The CDC’s travel wellness section also emphasizes that travelers should be counseled about possible side effects, interactions, and contamination, which is relevant because travel-related stress and diet changes can alter immune and nutrient needs [N3-F2].

## How infection type and setting influence results

Infection type and setting matter a lot. The strongest evidence is for colds, but the setting of the study influences results. In the general population, vitamin C did not reduce cold incidence [N6-R4]. In contrast, in people exposed to brief periods of severe physical exercise, vitamin C halved common cold risk [N3-F3]. This suggests that the benefit is more likely when the immune system is stressed or challenged [N3-F3].

For respiratory infections, the evidence is more indirect. The review of vitamin C and the common cold found that vitamin C may be useful for people exposed to brief periods of severe physical exercise, but not for routine prevention in the general population [N3-F3]. The Cochrane review also notes that only a few therapeutic trials have been carried out, so the evidence is still limited for specific treatment settings [N6-R4]. This means that the value of vitamin C may depend on whether the infection is mild and early-stage, versus severe or established.

Overall, vitamin C may matter most when infection risk is elevated by stress, physical strain, or deficiency. For colds, the evidence supports reduced duration and severity, especially with regular supplementation, but not routine prevention in the general population [N3-F3][N6-R4]. For respiratory infections more broadly, the evidence is less direct and more context-dependent, with some support for combined micronutrient use and limited evidence for higher-dose treatment [N6-R3][N3-F3].

The CDC’s travel wellness section explicitly warns that unproven therapies are discussed for educational purposes only and are not recommended [N3-F2]. It also notes that analyses of supplements sometimes find differences between labeled and actual ingredients, and that some products may contain illegal hidden ingredients such as prescription drugs [N3-F2]. A third misconception is that vitamin C can replace other lifestyle factors. The evidence shows that diet, stress, and other factors affect immune response [N1-F1][N3-F2]. So vitamin C is part of immune health, but it is not the only factor.

### 6. Bottom line

If you ask, “Does vitamin C daily help immunity?” the answer is: **yes, in a qualified way**. Vitamin C supports immune function and may reduce illness duration and severity, especially in colds and respiratory infections [N1-F1][N6-R4][N3-F3]. But it is **not a proven cure or standalone treatment** for infections, and it does not reliably prevent every illness [N6-R4][N4-R3].

So the best practical takeaway is:

- Eat a balanced diet rich in vitamin C first [N2-R3][N1-F1].
- Use supplements only when needed and not as a substitute for standard care [N3-F2][N6-R4].
- Keep doses below the upper limit of 2,000 mg/day unless a provider says otherwise [N2-R4].
- Know that vitamin C matters most when deficiency is present or when infection risk is elevated by stress, exercise, or other factors [N1-F1][N3-F3].

In short: vitamin C is part of immune health, but the evidence supports **supportive care**, not a magic cure [N1-F1][N6-R4].

The evidence repeatedly points to diet as a major determinant of immune status. The vitamin C and immune function review states that dietary intake of 100–200 mg/day provides adequate to saturating plasma concentrations and should cover general requirements [N1-F1]. It also notes that infections can significantly impact vitamin C levels due to enhanced inflammation and metabolic requirements, and that hypovitaminosis C is relatively common in Western populations [N1-F1]. - Eat a balanced diet rich in vitamin C first [N2-R3][N1-F1].
